specification.problem: Given N=p1 p2 and a coprime to N, find the order r (smallest r with a^r mod N = 1) via quantum order finding, then extract factors via gcds, including the case of odd r when a is a perfect square, which the abstract identifies as sometimes giving factors.
specification.reconstruction_scope: Minimal scoped construction: the classical number-theoretic relations of order-based factoring (even r, and odd r with square coprime a), plus the standard textbook phase-estimation form of order finding on the tiny instance N=15, a=4 (odd-order-type case with square coprime; order 2 is even, so a 4-style example is only illustrative). Outside the scope: the paper's two specific techniques (not discarding odd orders; searching for new order-finding relations after failure), the success-probability analysis, and any quantitative improvement estimates.

symbols.meaning: randomly chosen base coprime to N
multiplicative order of a modulo N
square root of a when a=b^2 is a perfect square
phase s/r estimated by phase estimation

equations.label: Order definition
equations.description: Definition of the order to be found by the QOFA.
equations.justification: The abstract defines the order this way.

equations.label: Factors from even order
equations.description: Factor extraction given even r; succeeds with probability at least 1/2 over random a, and may fail for some a (trivial factors).
equations.justification: Stated in the abstract; the success probability is also stated there.
assumptions: a^{r/2} not congruent to -1 mod N for nontrivial factors

equations.label: Odd order with square coprime
equations.description: If a is a perfect square, a^{r/2}=b^r is an integer even for odd r, so the gcd formulas can be evaluated; the factors are only sometimes nontrivial.
equations.abstract_quote: the factors can sometimes be found from odd orders if the coprime is square
equations.justification: Inferred from this claim: for a=b^2, a^{r/2}=b^r is an integer. The detailed form is my inference, not the paper's.
assumptions: a is a perfect square b^2
nontriviality of gcds is not guaranteed

equations.label: Phase estimation output for order finding
equations.description: Textbook QOFA: measured y/2^n approximates s/r for random s in {0..r-1}; r recovered by continued fractions. Approximation, not exact equality, unless r divides 2^n.
equations.justification: Standard Shor order-finding background; the abstract does not give these details.

equations.label: Continued fraction recovery
equations.description: Classical postprocessing to get a candidate r (denominator, possibly a divisor of r if gcd(s,r)>1).
equations.justification: Standard background; the paper's own relaxation/new-relation techniques are not reconstructed.

registers.name: counting
registers.role: phase estimation register holding x, then y after the QFT

specification.initial_state: |0>^{⊗n}|1> (counting register all zeros, work register encoding integer 1 in binary, little-endian assumed), then Hadamards on counting register.

steps.description: Choose a coprime to N (check gcd(a,N)=1); note whether a is a perfect square.
Prepare uniform superposition on counting register and apply controlled modular exponentiation to the work register.
Apply inverse QFT to the counting register and measure it to obtain y.
Use continued fractions on y/2^n to obtain candidate r; verify a^r mod N = 1.
If r even, compute gcds; if r odd and a=b^2, compute gcds with b^r; otherwise relaunch with a different a.

specification.measurement: Measure the counting register in the computational basis to obtain y; the work register may be left unmeasured.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Continued fraction expansion of y/2^n, order verification, then the gcd computations of eq_2 or eq_3; repeat with new a on failure.
assumptions: The scope is restricted to the standard QOFA plus the odd-order/square-coprime relation; the paper's two techniques are not reconstructed.
Counting register size 2^n >= N^2 is a standard choice, not from the abstract.
A tiny instance such as N=15 is suggested only for later testing; the abstract specifies none.
